facts.statement: Sinornis was described in 1992 as a 120-million-year-old sparrow-sized skeleton that combined primitive features with modern bird traits.
facts.quote: When it was described in 1992, this 120 million-year-old sparrow-sized skeleton represented a new avian sharing "primitive" features with Archaeopteryx as well as showing traits of modern birds.

facts.statement: Sinornis lived during the Lower Cretaceous period in the Jiufotang Formation of China.
facts.quote: Sinornis is a genus of enantiornithean birds from the Lower Cretaceous Jiufotang Formation of the People's Republic of China.

facts.statement: The Sinornis skeleton shares remarkable basal features with Archaeopteryx, an early transitional bird.
facts.quote: The skeleton exhibits remarkable basal features shared with Archaeopteryx, a genus of early bird that is transitional between older feathered dinosaurs and modern birds.

facts.statement: Sinornis possessed moderately recurved manual claws, which were less curved than the high-recurved claws of Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: Some of the primitive features found in Sinornis include moderately recurved manual unguals, as opposed to the high-recurved one in Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: Like Archaeopteryx, the pubis of Sinornis was directed ventrally and ended in a hook-shaped structure resembling a boot.
facts.quote: Analogous to Archaeopteryx and older theropod dinosaurs, its pubis appears to be directed more ventrally and terminates distally in a hook-shaped "boot".

facts.statement: The forelimb of Sinornis featured a separate carpus and manus, unlike the fused bones found in modern birds.
facts.quote: The postcranial skeleton features a separate carpus and manus in the forelimb.

facts.statement: The pelvis of Sinornis included a footed pubis bone.
facts.quote: The pelvis has a footed pubis.

facts.statement: Sinornis was capable of both perching and climbing.
facts.quote: Sinornis was also capable of perching and climbing.

facts.statement: Unlike modern birds, Sinornis had separate finger bones adapted for flight, and a reduced tail that shifted the center of gravity forward.
facts.quote: Unlike the fused finger bones of modern birds, Sinornis had separate finger bones that were well adapted for flight, while the reduction of the tail moved the centre of gravity forwards.

facts.statement: Originally, the Sinornis fossil was dated to about 135 million years ago, suggesting the transition to the modern wing occurred 15 million years after Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: The fossil of Sinornis was originally dated to about 135 million years, which seemed to show that about 15 million years after Archaeopteryx the transition to the modern wing was well underway.

facts.statement: Later research revised the age of the Sinornis fossil layers to 120 to 110 million years old, which reduced its perceived importance in the timeline of avian evolution.
facts.quote: However, later research showed that the layers in which the fossil was found were in fact about 120 to 110 million years old, reducing the importance of Sinornis.

facts.statement: Based on its skeleton, Sinornis shared flight and perching capabilities similar to modern sparrow-sized birds living in arboreal habitats.
facts.quote: Based on features present on the preserved skeleton of Sinornis, it shared similarity in flight performance and perching capabilities to sparrow-sized birds living today in arboreal habitats.

facts.statement: In 2001, Paul Sereno and colleagues considered the species Cathayornis to be a junior synonym of Sinornis due to their similar anatomy.
facts.quote: Paul Sereno et al. (2001) considered a similar prehistoric bird species from the same formation, Cathayornis, to be a junior synonym of Sinornis.

facts.statement: In 2001, Zhou and Hou argued that Cathayornis and Sinornis are distinct genera, citing differences in size, finger structure, and claw length.
facts.quote: However, also in 2001, Zhou and Hou continued to distinguish Cathayornis from Sinornis by the former's larger size, a shorter, straighter, finger number I, with a slightly longer claw (ungual), the absence of an atitrochanter, and other features.

facts.statement: Sinornis is classified within the subclass Enantiornithes.
facts.quote: subclassis: Enantiornithes

facts.statement: According to Swisher et al. (1999), the Jiufotang Formation where Sinornis was found suggests an age between the Aptian and Albian stages (100-120 million years ago).
facts.quote: La formación Jiufotang se superpone a la formación Yixian, lo que sugiere una edad entre el Aptiense al Albiense (entre hace 100-120 millones de años), de acuerdo a Swisher et al. (1999).

facts.statement: In 2001, researchers Paul Sereno and colleagues considered the prehistoric bird Cathayornis to be a junior synonym of Sinornis.
facts.quote: Paul Sereno et al. (2001) consideró a un ave prehistórica similar de la misma formación, Cathayornis, como un sinónimo más moderno de Sinornis.

facts.statement: In 2001, Zhou and Hou distinguished Cathayornis from Sinornis based on the larger size of the former, a shorter and straighter first digit with a slightly longer claw, and the absence of an atitrocánter.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, también en 2001 Zhou y Hou continuaron distinguiendo a Cathayornis de Sinornis debido al mayor tamaño del primero, y por tener un primer dígito más corto y recto con una uña levemente más larga (ungueal), la ausencia de un atitrocánter, entre otros rasgos.

facts.statement: Sinornis is classified within the parent group Enantiornithes.
facts.quote: Parent group: Enantiornithes

facts.statement: Sinornis is classified under the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Sinornis lived during the Aptian stage, between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (121.4 to 113.2 million years ago)

rejected.quote: Sinornis was capable of flight similar to modern birds based on breastbone and shoulder structures that provided both room and support for bulky aerobic flight muscles.

rejected.quote: The presence of a fully opposable hallux with a particularly large ungual and the pedal claws being strongly recurved are indicators of an advanced perching function and shows that the bird lived primarily in an arboreal habitat.

rejected.statement: A 2010 review by O'Connor and Dyke concluded that Sinornis and Cathayornis are not synonyms and differ in wing claw proportions, pelvic structure, and pygostyle size.
rejected.quote: O'Connor and Dyke concluded that despite the 2001 paper by Sereno and colleagues, the two birds were not synonyms and in fact differ in several clear ways, including different proportions in the wing claws and digits, differences in the pelvis, and size of the pygostyle.

rejected.statement: A 2010 review by Jingmai O'Connor and Gareth Dyke concluded that Sinornis and Cathayornis were not synonyms, differing in wing claw proportions, digit proportions, pelvic structure, and pygostyle size.
rejected.quote: O'Connor y Dyke concluyeron que a pesar del artículo de 2001 paper de Sereno y colegas, las dos aves no eran sinónimos y de hecho diferían de varias formas, incluyendo proporciones diferentes en las garras de las alas y los dígitos, diferencias en la pelvis, y el tamaño del pigóstilo.
